Best practice for component design
You can use the Raycast function to emit a ray in a certain direction in the scene and get the object it collides with.
An example: A 2-meter ray can be emitted forward from the player’s position every frame. If the ray collides with a wall, the player cannot move forward anymore.
There are two participants in raycasting: the one emitting the ray (A) and the one being collided with (B).
The code is written here for A;
A does not need a collider. B needs to have a collider.
Physics2D.Raycast is a function for implementing ray detection, and it stops when it collides with the first object.
It has an awful lot of optional parameters, and the more commonly used ones are:
RaycastHit2D Raycast(Vector2 origin, Vector2 direction, float distance, int layerMask)
origin: the starting position of the ray
direction: ray direction
distance: ray length
layermask: the layer involved in detection
</> Try using Raycast!

Recall: A field is another name for a variable in a class
Unity provides some field modifiers that change the way variables are displayed in the engine
Common Modifiers:

[Range(x,y)]		Make a variable display as a slider instead of an box

Sorting Layers
This represents the display hierarchy of objects. The higher the Sorting Layer, the "more front" the object is.
Note that this is completely different from the GameObject's layer!
Layer is used to classify objects, while Sorting Layer is used to control the display order.
Used to implement image masking
Make some images only display within the range of another image
Usage: Add the SpriteMask component to the masking object and set the MaskInteraction option in SpriteRenderer of themasked object.
Click on an image in the Project window to view its information
Each image has a type, such as Default, Sprite, Cursor, Normal Map, etc.
Note that if you want to use it in SpriteRenderer, you must select the Sprite type

Each image has a size limit (default is 2048x2048). You can roughly blur an image by modifying this limit. When importing a particularly large image (exceeding 2048), don't forget to increase the limit.

Open the Animation window: Windows>Animation
Function: Edit animations, create new animations
Each animation is an AnimationClip, stored in the Assets folder
The actual component that plays animations on an object is the Animator component
Open the Animator window: Windows>Animator
Function: Manage the playback order and logic of animations
Animation is defined by keyframes. We only need to modify the values of components on an object at several keyframes, and Unity will create a smooth transition between them to form an animation
What values can animations on an object affect?
All values that can be modified in the object's Inspector (position, color, variables we wrote ourselves, etc.)
All values on the child objects of this object
Note: Animations cannot affect child objects that already have an Animator component!
Only one animation can play on an object at a time
Using the Animation editor:
Select the desired frame
Click the record button
Adjust the values on the object's components
</> Let's create an animation that changes the position, rotation, scale and color of an object!
The priority of animation is higher than that of code!
For example: If an object is playing an animation that controls its position, no matter how we change its position in the code, it will not take effect
(Many "bugs" are caused by this)
</> Give it a try!
The Animator component is used to manage the order and logic of animation playback
Every object with animation has an AnimatorController (which can be viewed in the Animator component)
You can view and edit this AnimatorController in the Animator window
There are several important components in the Animator window:
States
Transitions
Variables
Layers
Each State represents an AnimationClip. When the Animator reaches a State, the animation corresponding to that State will be played
When a new animation is created, a State with the same name is automatically generated
View State information: Motion, Speed, Transitions
The orange State is the starting State
The Animator will directly play the animation of this State when the game starts running. An Animator has exactly one starting State.
You can right-click to select any State to be the starting State.
Transition defines the way we switch/transition between States
The white arrow connecting two States is a Transition
You can right-click to choose to create a Transition between any two States
View the properties of Transition:
Exit Time – At what time does the current clip start transitioning to the next clip?
Transition Duration – How long does the transition take?
Interruption Source – What other transitions can interrupt this transition?
Variables in the Animator are used to control the occurrence of Transitions. For example, the transition to the jump animation should only happen when we press the spacebar
Variables can be managed in the panel on the left
Animator offers several variable types: float, int, bool, trigger. Among them, bool and trigger are the most commonly used
bool: that is, a boolean value. It can be set to true or false
trigger: is a boolean value that is true for an instant. It then becomes invalid immediately afterwards
You can add variable conditions at the bottom of the Transition panel. When the conditions are not met, the Animator will stay in the current State; otherwise, it will execute the Transition
</> Let's add variable conditions to the transition!
We can modify the values of variables in Animator within the code to control the playback of animations
Common APIs:
animator.SetBool(string name, bool value)
animator.SetTrigger(string name)
(Why is it written as animator here instead of Animator?)
</> Use these APIs to control animations!
Easier animation playback:
animator.Play(string stateName)
This method is suitable for situations where smooth transitions are not required (such as 2D frame animations)
Overload:
animator.Play(string stateName, int layer, float normalizedTime)
For example, "play a state from the beginning": "animator.Play(stateName, 0, 0)"
Use Unity's animation system to try creating some animations and connect them!
The Camera component provides the function of viewing from a position at an angle and rendering the seen image on the screen or texture.
Cameras have two main modes: Perspective and Orthographic
Perspective Camera:
Objects appear larger when close and smaller when far away, which is generally used in 3D games.
The field of view is a cone (viewing frustum). Objects between the Near Plane and Far Plane can be seen.
Field of View: the width of the viewing frustum
Orthographic Camera:
Objects appear the same size regardless of their distance, and this is generally used in 2D games.
The field of view is a rectangular prism.
Size: the size of the field of view
A scene can have more than one camera!
The Camera component has the following common parameters related to color rendering:
Clear Flags: Defines what the camera needs to display in empty areas (where there are no objects)
Skybox: Display the skybox
Solid Color: Displays a single color
Depth Only: Displays nothing (transparent)
Don’t Clear: Keep the last frame
BackgroundColor: The color displayed in the background when in Clear Flags mode
Culling Mask: The layer rendered by this camera
Depth: the layer order of the camera itself; cameras with a larger Depth will be rendered on top
</> How to render a scene with two cameras together? What are the benefits of doing this?
